1016.title: Stephen of Hungary (16 August)
1016.hook: the king Hungarians remember as their first Christian king
1016.howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of Saint Stephen of Hungary on 16 August; in Hungary his feast is kept on 20 August as a national holiday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pontian and Hippolytus, a pope and his rival at peace in the mines. Your line was reconciled in the mines.

In a parliament building in Budapest, under guard, sits a golden crown. Enamel pictures of saints. Pearls hanging on little chains. And on top, a small cross that sits crooked, bent at an angle, and nobody has straightened it. Hungarians call it the Holy Crown, and they link it to the name of one king. For a long time, tradition says, no one counted as king of Hungary unless crowned with it. Today, the man whose name the crown carries.
screen: `A GOLDEN CROWN UNDER GUARD.` → `A CROOKED CROSS.` → `ONE KING'S NAME.`

segments.voice: Stephen was born the son of a Magyar ruler, at a time when his people were turning from their old gods. Tradition says he was baptized young and took the name Stephen. When he came to power, he wanted to be a Christian king, and tradition says he asked the pope for his blessing and received a crown. Hungarians remember him as their first Christian king. He built churches and organized the Church across his land. He also had to fight to hold it together, and the stories don't pretend he was gentle with every rival. One personal thing he left is a letter of advice to his son, Emeric, which tradition keeps as Stephen's admonitions. As it's usually summarized, he tells his son to keep the faith, to pray, to be patient and merciful, to listen to good counsel, and to welcome strangers, because they bring new gifts to a land. A king writing to the boy who would be king after him. Then grief. Emeric died young, before his father. Stephen, with no heir, is said to have offered his crown and his people to Mary. So the crown is the thread. A crown is power. It can also be a promise, given in trust and handed on. The scriptures speak of another kind of crown, the one at the end of a faithful life. In the Douay-Rheims, Paul writes: "there is laid up for me a crown of justice." Stephen wore one crown, and tradition says he hoped for the other.
screen: `A RULER'S SON, BAPTIZED.` · `A CROWN AND A KINGDOM.` · `ADVICE TO HIS SON.` · `A CROWN HANDED TO MARY.` · then, large: `A CROWN OF JUSTICE.`

segments.voice: Bring Hungary to mind, its towns and rivers, its people getting up this morning for work and school; you don't have to know much, just keep them company. If you pray, pray for its people, its leaders and its families; if you don't, wish them well, breath by breath. If Hungary feels far away, add the place you live, and hold both.
Admonitions. The letter of advice Stephen, Hungary's first Christian king, wrote to his son Emeric, telling him to keep the faith, be patient and merciful, and welcome strangers.
Your line: the holy crown. Some of what we hold is only ours to keep for someone else. See you tomorrow.

1017.title: The Queenship of Mary (22 August)
1017.hook: a week after the Assumption, Mary honored as queen
1017.howItsDone: On 22 August Catholics keep the memorial of the Queenship of Mary; Catholics pray the Salve Regina, one of the Marian antiphons that can close Night Prayer, and the last glorious mystery of the rosary is her coronation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Stephen of Hungary and his admonitions, a king's advice to his son. Your line was the holy crown.

A week ago the Church kept the Assumption: Mary, taken body and soul into heaven. In the rosary, the very next glorious mystery, the last one, is a coronation. It turns up in paintings and stained glass: gold, stars, and a crown lowered onto Mary's head by her Son. Yesterday's crown sat on a king. Today's sits on a woman from a small town who married a carpenter. So why call her a queen at all? And what kind of queen would she be?
screen: `A WEEK AFTER THE ASSUMPTION.` → `THE LAST GLORIOUS MYSTERY.` → `WHY A QUEEN?`

segments.voice: Start with the Gospel. Before Jesus is born, the angel tells Mary about her son, in the Douay-Rheims: "and of his kingdom there shall be no end." A king. Catholics reason from that in one short step: the mother of the king is the queen. When Mary visits her cousin, Elizabeth greets her: "whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Second, the old kingdom of Israel. When Bathsheba comes to her son, King Solomon, he rises to meet her and has a throne set for the king's mother, "and she sat on his right hand." And she came to ask a favor for someone else. Catholics read Mary in that seat: not ruling in her Son's place, but near him, bringing other people's requests. Third, the Apocalypse, the Bible's last book: "a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet, and on her head a crown of twelve stars." Readers have heard Israel in that woman, or the Church; Catholic tradition also hears Mary. Fourth, what kind of queen. Catholic teaching is careful here. Mary is not a goddess. She is a creature, like everyone else, honored because of her Son. Her crown is a mother's crown. That's why the old hymn, the Salve Regina, greets her as queen and, in the same breath, as mother of mercy. The two titles explain each other. Other Christians honor Mary in other ways, and some don't use this title at all.

1018.title: Bartholomew (24 August)
1018.hook: the apostle often identified with Nathanael, a man without guile
1018.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Bartholomew, apostle, on 24 August; the Gospel read at Mass that day is the calling of Nathanael from the first chapter of John.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Queenship of Mary, honored as queen because she is the mother of the King. Your line was queen and mother.

"Can any thing of good come from Nazareth?" Those are Nathanael's first words about Jesus, before they've even met. His friend Philip has just found him with big news: we have found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael answers with a put-down of the man's hometown. It's rude. It's also completely honest. And Philip doesn't argue. He just says three words: come and see. Today, the apostle kept on the twenty-fourth of August, and the honest skeptic who may be the same man.
screen: `CAN ANY THING OF GOOD COME FROM NAZARETH?` → `PHILIP DOESN'T ARGUE.` → `COME AND SEE.`

segments.voice: First, a puzzle. Matthew, Mark and Luke list a Bartholomew among the twelve apostles, named right beside Philip, but never tell a single story about him. John never uses the name Bartholomew at all. Instead, John tells about Nathanael, brought to Jesus by Philip. So tradition puts the two together: one man. Nobody can prove it. It's a reasoned guess, held openly, and the Church reads this very story on his feast. Now the story. Before Nathanael can say anything, Jesus says of him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom there is no guile." Guile is an old word for trickery: a hidden angle, saying one thing and meaning another. Jesus doesn't scold him for the crack about Nazareth. He names what was good in it: a man with nothing hidden. Nathanael is startled: how do you know me? Jesus says he saw him under the fig tree, before Philip ever called him. The Gospel never says what happened under that fig tree. Whatever it was, it lands. Nathanael's doubt turns, on the spot, into faith: "Rabbi, thou art the Son of God." Same honesty, new direction. Tradition adds that Bartholomew preached far from home and died a martyr, by some accounts flayed alive, which is why paintings sometimes show him holding a knife. The Gospels don't tell any of that. What they keep is one moment: an honest doubter, a friend who said come and see, and a man without guile.

1019.title: Joseph Calasanz (25 August)
1019.hook: he opened the first free public school in Europe (1597)
1019.tomorrow: The death of John the Baptist (29 August)
1019.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Joseph Calasanz on 25 August; Piarist schools and parishes honor him as their founder, and Catholic teachers ask his prayers for their students.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bartholomew, the honest doubter who heard come and see. Your line was without guile.

Joseph Calasanz came to Rome, the story goes, hoping for a good church post. A priest from Spain, with plans. Then he started noticing the children in the poor streets: running loose, working, getting into trouble. None of them in school, because school cost money and their families had none. He asked the parish to teach them. No room. He asked others. Nobody took it on. So he did it himself: he found rooms, gathered the children, and taught them reading, writing, sums and the faith, and charged nothing. The good church post never mattered again.
screen: `A PRIEST WITH PLANS.` → `CHILDREN WITH NO SCHOOL.` → `SO HE DID IT HIMSELF.`

segments.voice: He called them the Pious Schools, and the order he founded to run them is known as the Piarists. The idea was simple and, for its time, bold: a poor child's mind is worth teaching, properly, and for free. Not charity on the side. Real lessons, every day, alongside prayer. Jesus says in the Douay-Rheims: "he that shall receive one such little child in my name, receiveth me." Calasanz took that literally. Every child at the door was a guest of that kind. The schools grew, and other teachers joined. Then, near the end of his life, the story turns hard. Men inside his own order worked against him. He was removed from leading it, and the order itself was cut down and stripped of its standing. Everything he had built looked finished. Tradition remembers that he didn't fight it with bitterness. He kept praying, kept obeying, kept teaching where he could, and forgave the men who had done it. He died with the work in ruins. After his death, the order was restored, and the schools went on. The Church later named him a patron of Christian schools. So the lesson has two halves. Everyone deserves an education, including the child whose family can't pay. And when the good thing you built is taken from you, Calasanz's answer, in the story, was patience, and it outlived the men who opposed him.
screen: `THE PIOUS SCHOOLS.` · `RECEIVE ONE SUCH LITTLE CHILD.` · `TURNED ON BY HIS OWN.` · `RESTORED AFTER HIS DEATH.` · then, large: `FREE SCHOOLS.`

1020.title: The death of John the Baptist (29 August)
1020.hook: the prophet dies for telling a king the truth
1020.howItsDone: On 29 August Catholics keep the Passion of Saint John the Baptist; the Gospel at Mass that day tells his death from the sixth chapter of Mark.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph Calasanz, who taught children whose families couldn't pay. Your line was free schools.

The party is already loud. It's King Herod's birthday, and around his table sit his lords, his officers, the leading men of Galilee. Somewhere under his power sits a prisoner: a man who once wore camel hair by the Jordan, whom the king has locked up but can't bring himself to kill. Then a girl comes in and dances, and the king is so pleased that he makes a promise out loud, in front of everyone: ask me for whatever you want, up to half my kingdom. She goes out to ask her mother what to ask for.
screen: `A KING'S BIRTHDAY.` → `A PRISONER HE WON'T KILL.` → `A PROMISE IN FRONT OF EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Mark tells it in his sixth chapter. Herod had married Herodias, his brother's wife, and John had said to him, in the Douay-Rheims: "It is not lawful for thee to have thy brother's wife." That's the whole offense. One sentence, and true. Herodias wanted him dead. Herod didn't, not quite. Mark gives a strange, honest detail: Herod feared John, "knowing him to be a just and holy man," and liked to listen to him. So the king kept the prophet locked up, and kept coming back to hear him. Then the dance, and the promise. The girl's mother tells her what to ask for: the head of John the Baptist. The girl hurries back and adds: on a dish. Mark says the king was struck with sorrow. But he had sworn, his guests were watching, and he couldn't stand to back down at his own party. So he sent the executioner. Afterward, John's disciples came, took his body, and laid it in a tomb. Notice who is free in this story. The king has the throne and the power, and he's trapped by an oath he made to look generous. The prisoner has nothing, and he's the one person in the room who said what was true. The Church calls this day the passion of John the Baptist, the same word it uses for the suffering of Christ. All his life John went ahead of Jesus, preparing the way. Catholics see him going ahead of Jesus here, too.

1021.title: Jeanne Jugan (30 August)
1021.hook: a poor Frenchwoman who took an old blind woman into her own bed and founded the Little Sisters of the Poor
1021.tomorrow: The Holy Name of Mary (12 September)
1021.howItsDone: Catholics keep the memory of Saint Jeanne Jugan on 30 August; the Little Sisters of the Poor, the congregation she began, run homes for poor elderly people and go out asking for alms to support them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the death of John the Baptist, the prophet killed for one true sentence. Your line was truth cost his head.

A narrow staircase. A small room. One bed. Jeanne Jugan is a poor woman in a seaside town in Brittany, in France, earning her keep with her hands. One winter, the story goes, she comes home carrying an old woman who is blind, widowed, and has nowhere to go. Jeanne carries her up the stairs, lays her in her own bed, and takes the attic for herself. That's how it begins. Not with a plan, or a building, or money. With one bed, given away. Today, the woman behind the Little Sisters of the Poor.
screen: `A STAIRCASE, A ROOM, ONE BED.` → `A BLIND OLD WOMAN, NOWHERE TO GO.` → `HER OWN BED, GIVEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: One old woman became two, then more. A few younger women joined Jeanne, and they called themselves sisters. But they had nothing to feed anyone with. So Jeanne picked up a basket and went begging, door to door, for her old people: food, coins, scraps, whatever people would give. Tradition remembers her knocking, being refused, and coming back. It wasn't humiliating to her, the story goes; it was the work. The community grew into the Little Sisters of the Poor, homes where the poor and the old could live and die with someone beside them. Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "as long as you did it to one of these my least brethren, you did it to me." Jeanne lived that line one bed at a time. Then the hidden half of her story. A priest who helped direct the young community took control of it. Jeanne, the founder, was removed as its head and sent to live quietly in the motherhouse, doing small tasks among the novices. For a long time, the young sisters arriving weren't told that she had begun it all. She didn't fight it. Tradition remembers her telling the novices to be little, and to stay little. Only later was she recognized as the founder, and later still the Church named her a saint. So her life gives the word old two meanings: the old people she served, and her own old age, spent hidden, with nothing to show for what she'd built. Catholics see both as given to God.

Jeanne Jugan. The poor Frenchwoman who gave her own bed to a blind old woman, begged door to door for her old people, and began the Little Sisters of the Poor.

1022.title: The Holy Name of Mary (12 September)
1022.hook: a feast of her name, restored in 2002
1022.howItsDone: Catholics may keep the optional memorial of the Most Holy Name of Mary on 12 September, and honor her name whenever they pray the Hail Mary, which joins the angel's greeting to her name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeanne Jugan, who gave her own bed to a blind old woman. Your line was for the old.

"And the virgin's name was Mary." Luke saves it for the end of the sentence. First the angel, Gabriel. Then the town, Nazareth. Then the man she is promised to, Joseph, of the house of David. And then, last, almost quietly, her name. Today the Church gives a whole feast to that last word. Not to something Mary did, or a moment in her life. Just to her name. It's also the end of a week of saints, so there's a look back at them, too.
screen: `THE ANGEL, THE TOWN, JOSEPH.` → `THEN, LAST: HER NAME.` → `A FEAST FOR A NAME.`

segments.voice: Start with the name itself. It's an old name. In the Douay-Rheims, Moses's sister, who sang by the sea, carries it too: "Mary the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel in her hand." So the girl in Nazareth carried a name that was already old, a name with a song in it. What does it mean? Readers over the centuries have offered guesses. Luke doesn't say. Second, who says her name. In Luke the angel's greeting is "Hail, full of grace," with no name at all. A moment later, when she's troubled, he says it: "Fear not, Mary, for thou hast found grace with God." Her name arrives with comfort. Third, why a feast for a name. Catholics hear a name as standing for the whole person. The Church already honors the Holy Name of Jesus, and this feast does the same for his mother: for Catholics, to say her name with love is to turn toward her. In the Hail Mary, they put her name back into the angel's greeting. This feast has been on the Church's general calendar, off it for a time, and back again. And now, the week. Stephen of Hungary, and the holy crown. The Queenship of Mary, queen and mother. Bartholomew, without guile. Joseph Calasanz, and his free schools. John the Baptist, whose truth cost his head. Jeanne Jugan, for the old. And today, one name.
screen: `MOSES'S SISTER, WHO SANG BY THE SEA.` · `FEAR NOT, MARY.` · `A NAME STANDS FOR THE PERSON.` · `A WEEK OF SAINTS.` · then, large: `AND THE VIRGIN'S NAME WAS MARY.`

segments.voice: On an out-breath, say her name once, aloud or inside, Mary, then let it rest and breathe a few times before you say it again, adding nothing. If you pray, pray the Hail Mary slowly and pause where her name comes; if you don't, think of how your own name sounds when someone who loves you says it, and let that be enough.
